issues.legal_issue: A conviction may rest on reliable oral and recorded dying-declaration evidence despite defects in the formal recording of the declaration.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness to the attack, but the injured person was conscious and able to speak after being stabbed.
Several witnesses testified that the injured person identified the principal attacker as the person who stabbed him.
A police officer recorded the injured person’s statement at the scene shortly after the attack, and the statement was later treated as a dying declaration.
The injury described in the statements was corroborated by medical evidence.

The investigating officer did not separately record a dying declaration or have a doctor establish the injured person’s fitness to make a statement; the injured person died more than 24 hours after the attack.
issues.conclusion: The conviction of the principal attacker was upheld because the dying-declaration evidence was reliable and corroborated, notwithstanding the investigating officer’s omissions.
issues.legal_principle: A statement made by an injured person may be relied on as a dying declaration even if it was recorded as an ordinary police statement rather than expressly as a dying declaration, where the evidence establishes that the person was conscious and fit to speak and the statement is reliable. Investigative omissions should not automatically benefit the accused; the prosecution evidence must be assessed apart from those omissions. The Court relied on Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar and others, J.T. (1998) 3 SC 290, and upheld the conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction is appealed and a conscious injured person’s identification is recounted by multiple witnesses, recorded by police at the scene, and medically corroborated, the conviction may be upheld despite the investigator’s failure to formally record a dying declaration.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for participation in a fatal assault under a common-intention theory cannot stand when the evidence about the alleged participants’ roles is materially inconsistent and there is no direct evidence.
material_facts: The alleged participants were convicted of the fatal assault on the basis of common intention.
There was no direct evidence of the attack.
Witnesses recounted inconsistent accounts of the injured person’s statements about the alleged participants: some said they surrounded him, some said they struck him, and others said they held him.
The evidence consistently identified the principal attacker as the person who stabbed the injured person, but did not reliably establish the roles of the alleged participants.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the alleged participants under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code were set aside because their guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.
issues.legal_principle: Common-intention liability requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of the accused persons’ guilt. Where there is no direct evidence and the dying-declaration accounts are inconsistent about the alleged participants’ roles, their convictions under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code cannot be sustained.
